frames.narration: Someone in a crowded city centre asks for ramen, open now, within 1 km. The app sends the location, the radius and the filters to the Search API.

messages.label: ramen, open now, 1 km, at my location

frames.narration: The API rounds the location to about 100 m and builds a cache key from it, the radius and the filters. Nobody has asked this exact question in the last few minutes, so it is a miss.

messages.label: key: spot + ramen + open now + 1 km

frames.narration: The request goes to the search service of that region, which asks its index replica for the places inside the circle. The quadtree starts at the root and only descends into squares that touch the circle.

The leaves are small here because the area is crowded. The index measured the distance to 3,100 places and 2,480 are inside the circle, so about 600 were examined for nothing. A full scan of 200 million would have measured every place.

The entries carry category and opening hours, so the search service drops everything that is not ramen and open now. Of 2,480 places, 61 remain. They are scored by relevance, smoothed rating, popularity and distance.
The top 20 go back with a cursor for the next page. The API stores the list in the cache for a few minutes and answers the phone.
A minute later someone standing 40 m away asks for the same thing. The rounded location is the same, so the cache has the answer and the index is not touched.
Meanwhile an owner changes the closing time of their restaurant. The API writes it to the places database, and the change is also put on the queue in the same transaction.

Every replica of that region reads the event and updates the entry in place. Within about a minute the new hours are used by the open-now filter, and cached results that include the place expire within a few minutes.
